title: Auth: sessions vs JWT
summary: Server-side sessions versus stateless JWTs: where the trust lives, how each scales, revocation and logout trade-offs, and a Java sketch of both.
note:
1. Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you may do
2. Session: server stores state, client holds an opaque session id in a cookie
3. JWT: signed token carries the claims, server stores nothing
4. Trade-off: sessions revoke instantly but need a store; JWTs scale statelessly but are hard to revoke before expiry
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: Why is a JWT hard to revoke?
recall.a: It is self-contained and valid until it expires; the server keeps no record of it, so you need a denylist or short expiry + refresh tokens to cut it off early.

recall.q: Where does the trust live in a session scheme?
recall.a: On the server — the cookie holds only an opaque id; all the real data sits in the session store.

recall.q: One security flag every auth cookie should have?
recall.a: HttpOnly (plus Secure and SameSite) so client JavaScript cannot read the token.

shot.title: Sessions vs JWT
shot.body:
| | Session | JWT |
|---|---|---|
| server state | yes (store) | none |
| scaling | needs shared store | stateless |
| revoke | instant | hard (denylist/expiry) |
| payload | opaque id | signed claims |
| typical use | server-rendered apps | APIs, microservices |

sections.title: Authn vs authz
sections.body: ✍️ **Authentication** proves identity (login). **Authorization** decides permissions (can this user delete that order?). Both schemes below solve the 'how do we remember you logged in' problem across HTTP's stateless requests.

sections.title: Server-side sessions
sections.body: ✍️ On login the server creates a session record (in memory, Redis, or a DB) and sends the client an opaque **session id** in an `HttpOnly` cookie. Each request the server looks the id up to find the user. Revoking is trivial — delete the record. Cost: every server needs to reach a shared session store, or you pin users to one server.

sections.title: Stateless JWTs
sections.body:
✍️ A **JSON Web Token** is `header.payload.signature`; the signature (HMAC or RSA) lets any server verify the claims without a lookup. The server stores nothing, which scales cleanly across many instances. The catch: you cannot easily invalidate a token before it expires.
- Mitigation: short-lived access tokens + a longer refresh token, or a small revocation denylist.
